newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich sees new strategy for Medicare next year.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich sees new strategy for Medicare next year.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Wednesday Republicans will leave the prickly issue of Medicare reform to a bipartisan commission next year if they still control Congress after Tuesday's election.

In a striking departure from the partisan strategy that led to two government shutdowns last winter, Gingrich told Reuters it was a mistake to leave the huge federal health-care programme to a political battle with President Clinton.

"We need a bipartisan commission to take it out of politics, a very short commission, maybe 90 days or something," he said when asked how his party would handle Medicare if it retains its majority in Congress.
"My advice would be to go to a commission to get it out of politics and to have some common understanding and some common agreement on what needs to be done," the Georgia Republican added.

Gingrich also said he plans to take charge next year of a "positive" new diabetes programme aimed at educating the elderly about the effects of a disease linked to 27 percent of all Medicare costs. "It's a huge, huge factor. This to me is something I'll really focus on early," he said.

Both Democrats and Republicans agree that the financially troubled Medicare programme needs reform. On Monday, the Clinton administration said the Medicare trust fund that pays hospitals for the elderly had registered a $4.2 billion deficit for the last fiscal year.

But Gingrich, cast by Democrats as poster boy for unpopular Republican policies, has been stung by criticism over Medicare from within his party in the waning days of the campaign. The issue has contributed to Clinton's double-digit lead over Republican Bob Dole in opinion polls, while some surveys have given Democrats an edge in races for the Senate and the House.

Republican vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp was quoted this week as saying Gingrich's handling of Medicare reform during the budget standoff with Clinton sent the wrong signal and left the party on the defensive.
But Gingrich Wednesday dismissed suggestions of a rift with Kemp less than a week before the election and continued to blame Clinton's budget veto for shutting the government.
"Jack and (Kemp's wife) Joanne both called my wife yesterday to say this ... story's exaggerated. Jack and I are very close personal friends," he said.

"The only reason we were ever on the defensive was that Democrats didn't tell the truth. There's no question that Clinton out-manoeuvred us in the budget fight and there's no question that we underestimated their willingness to lie about Medicare," he added.

Despite speculation that Republicans could lose the House and Senate Nov. 5, ending his two-year tenure as speaker, Gingrich said he was increasingly optimistic about his party's chances of keeping control of both chambers.

"The odds are literally nine to one, or better, that I'll be speaker," he said. "The odds are overwhelming that we're going to keep the House ... There are more Democrats in trouble right now than Republicans."

He said Republican House and Senate candidates have met with suprising success in Northeastern states. "If you were seeing an anti-Republican tide, that's the region you'd see it really show itself in. And yet there are three states where we have really competitive Senate races."
